title: Concurrency bottleneck mapping for LLM inference
summary: Working notes from exploratory experiments that map how increasing concurrent request load interacts with tensor/pipeline parallel regions, NCCL saturation, and per-GPU utilization for a family of 13B and 34B models. Goal: identify clear signals to drive autoscaler and fallback routing heuristics.
content:
Purpose:
This doc records a set of controlled experiments to understand how concurrency (parallel in-flight requests) interacts with multi-GPU serving for medium-large autoregressive models. We want to surface deterministic bottlenecks (comm, compute, scheduling) and produce actionable heuristics for the runtime: when to increase batching, when to drop to a smaller variant, and when to steer traffic away from a node due to interconnect saturation.

High-level hypothesis:
1) At low concurrency, throughput is compute-bound and good NVLink/PCIe headroom exists.
2) As concurrency increases, asynchronous KV-cache pressure and PCIe transfers for KV flushes create periodic bursts that coincide with NCCL collectives during attention phases, leading to latency tail spikes.
3) Pipeline-parallel padding (uneven micro-batch distribution) amplifies sync waits — more so for models with shallow pipeline stages.

Experiment matrix (summary):
- Models: rwd-13B-fp16, rwd-34B-fp16 (same architecture family, different shard counts).
- Parallel configs: TP-only (tensor parallel 2/4), PP-only (pipeline 2/4), TP+PP mixed (TP=2, PP=2).
- Network: DGX-A100 style NVLink mesh (full bisection) vs. Ethernet+PCIe host (simulated by toggling NCCL P2P and limiting interconnect).
- Concurrency sweep: 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 concurrent requests.
- Request shape: greedy decode, prompt lengths {16, 64}, generation length 128 tokens.

Instrumentation and signals captured:
- nvprof / nsight metrics: SM utilization, DRAM throughput, kernel durations.
- nvidia-smi sampling (1s): GPU memory, %util, encoder/decoder kernel names.
- NCCL_TRACE and NCCL_P2P_LEVEL logs parsed for bandwidth and synchronization windows.
- Runtime traces: per-request span durations, queue time, batch-assembly time, KV cache hits/evictions.
- Packet-capture style counters: PCIe bytes transferred per-step (approximated via driver counters).

Representative findings:
1) Low concurrency (1–4):
   - rwd-13B in TP=2 shows steady throughput ~210 tokens/s per-GPU, p50 latency ~180ms. NVLink utilization ~45% (headroom).
   - rwd-34B with PP=2 has slightly higher p50 due to pipeline stage skew but stable p95.

2) Medium concurrency (8–16):
   - Sudden divergence between throughput and expected linear scaling. Measured tokens/sec per-GPU increases sublinearly with concurrency past 8.
   - NCCL windows show frequent small collectives (all-reduce and reduce-scatter) with reduced effective bandwidth (~40% of theoretical) due to contention with host-to-device transfers for KV cache state.
   - Observed pattern: many requests complete their compute kernels but then sit waiting in a synchronization barrier while another request triggers a large PCIe flush. Tail latency spikes correspond to those barriers.

3) High concurrency (32):
   - NVLink counters approach saturation on the worst links; per-step bandwidth oscillates wildly.
   - GPUs report transient memory pressure as KV caches evict; this causes extra host roundtrips that serialize with NCCL.
   - p95 latency balloons (2–4x) and overall tokens/sec sometimes regresses compared to concurrency 16 due to starvation and backpressure.

Micro-observations and oddities:
- On TP-only configs, the library’s kernel fusion helps hide some communication but only when batch composition aligns (micro-batches of uniform length). Varied prompt lengths break fusion and expose many small NCCL collectives.
- Pipeline stages with unbalanced operator counts create deterministic hold-ups: the longer stage becomes a choke point; increasing micro-batch interleaving reduced this but at cost of more frequent small collectives.
- Enabling CUDA IPC between processes reduced PCIe traffic but increased CPU scheduling pressure and sometimes increased jitter for small requests.

Profiles and snippets (textual):
- Example NCCL snapshot (TP+PP, concurrency=16, rwd-34B):
  - reduce-scatter: avg size 1.2MB, avg latency 2.8ms, occuring every decode step; effective bandwidth ~35GB/s vs link peak 63GB/s.
  - all-reduce: bursts aligned to positional embedding updates; several microseconds of idle before collective start.

- Runtime trace example: request X -> queue wait 12ms, batch assembly 5ms, compute kernels 48ms, KV flush 3ms, NCCL wait 26ms, output serialize 2ms.

Implications for autoscaler and routing heuristics:
- Trigger autoscale-up on sustained NVLink > 70% and NCCL effective bandwidth > 60% of measured baseline for >30s. This is a better signal than GPU %util which lags.
- Prefer routing short prompt, short-generation traffic to nodes with low concurrent KV cache usage (we measured 3–5x lower tail when KV cache contention is low).
- For mixed prompt-length workloads, enable micro-batch homogenization in the batcher (delay short prompts briefly to coalesce) — reduces small collective count and p95 at cost of minimal median increase.
- When pipeline imbalance detected (per-stage avg compute time variance > 25%), trigger interleaved scheduling or recommend TP adjustments.

Quick recommended action items:
1) Add NVLink/NCCL derived signals to per-node telemetry with 10s resolution (NVLink bytes/s, NCCL effective BW, host->device PCIe bytes).
2) Implement a conservative routing rule: if NCCL_eff_bw > 60% and concurrency > 8, prefer lower-concurrency nodes or fall back to a smaller model variant.
3) Prototype micro-batch homogenizer inside the assembler with two knobs: delay_threshold_ms and max_coalesce_count. Run ablation to quantify median vs p95 trade.
4) Add a small experiment to test CUDA IPC vs host PCIe tradeoff across mixed-length prompts and document CPU scheduling overhead.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How general are these observations across different vendor topologies (A100 vs H100 vs other meshes)? Need matched experiments.
- Can we modify NCCL tuning parameters (ring vs tree, algorithmic thresholds) dynamically in the runtime? Risks and gain quantification required.
- Is it viable to offload KV cache spill handling to a co-located CPU process to avoid interfering with NCCL windows?

Appendix: raw commands used (abridged)
- launcher invocation: ./run_inference_bench --model rwd-13B --tp 2 --pp 2 --concurrency 16 --prompt-shape 64 --gen 128 --trace-level perf
- NCCL logs: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=SYS ./run_inference_bench ...
- perf counters: sudo nvidia-smi nvlink --query-gpu=nvlink.bandwidth --format=csv

Notes to reviewers:
- These are early experiments; some numbers vary with kernel versions and driver combinations. Please check GH PR redwood/serve-runtime#487 for the instrumentation code and INF-1123 for the autoscaler feature request.
- I expect the micro-batch homogenizer to be the lowest-effort high-impact mitigation for p95.

Signed-off-by: Maya
footnotes: Hardware: DGX-like nodes with 8x A100 NVLink mesh and a fallback host-only cluster with 4x GPUs per node behind PCIe
